text: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven SI base quantities?
explanation: Force is a derived quantity (= mass × acceleration); the seven SI base quantities are length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.

text: The SI unit of luminous intensity is the:
explanation: The candela (cd) is the SI base unit of luminous intensity.

text: 1 nanometre equals:
explanation: The prefix 'nano' = 10⁻⁹.

text: The number of significant figures in 0.007 m² is:
explanation: Leading zeros are never significant; only the digit 7 is significant, so 0.007 has 1 significant figure (matches the textbook's own answer key, Ex 1.10(a)).

text: In the equation v = u + at, dimensional analysis shows 'at' must have the same dimensions as:
explanation: Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added; since v and u are velocities, 'at' must also have dimensions of velocity [LT⁻¹].

text: A physical quantity P is calculated from P = a²b³/c, where a, b, c are measured with percentage errors 1%, 2%, 3% respectively. The percentage error in P is:
explanation: For a product/quotient of powers, percentage errors add weighted by their exponents: ΔP/P×100 = 2(1%) + 3(2%) + 1(3%) = 2+6+3 = 11%.

text: If the unit of mass is doubled, unit of length is halved, and unit of time is unchanged, the unit of kinetic energy (½mv²) changes by a factor of:
explanation: KE ∝ mass × velocity² ∝ mass × length²/time²: factor = 2 × (1/2)² × 1 = 2 × 1/4 = 1/2.

text: Which measuring instrument gives the least count directly related to its pitch and number of circular-scale divisions?
explanation: A screw gauge's least count = pitch ÷ number of divisions on the circular (head) scale.

text: The dimensional formula of the gravitational constant G is:
explanation: From F = Gm₁m₂/r², G = Fr²/(m₁m₂), giving [MLT⁻²][L²]/[M²] = [M⁻¹L³T⁻²].

text: A calorie equals 4.2 J, where 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻². In a system where the unit of mass is α kg, length β m and time γ s, a calorie has magnitude:
explanation: Matching dimensions [M L² T⁻²] under unit change n′ = n(u/u′): the new numeric value is 4.2 α⁻¹β⁻²γ² (textbook Ex 1.3).

text: The order of magnitude of the diameter of a hydrogen atom is about:
explanation: An atom's size is of order 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m.

text: A boy recalls the relativistic mass relation but forgets where to place the speed of light c. The dimensionally correct form of m = m₀(1 − v²)⁻¹ᐟ² is:
explanation: v²/c² must be dimensionless for the bracket to make sense, so c must appear as v²/c² (textbook Ex 1.13).

text: Which of these is the most precise way to measure the thickness of a human hair?
options: An optical microscope measuring to within a wavelength of light
explanation: An optical instrument resolving to within a wavelength of visible light (~500 nm) is far more precise than mechanical vernier/screw devices for something as thin as a hair.

text: 'To call a quantity large or small is meaningless without specifying a standard of comparison' — this best illustrates:
options: the need for a reference/standard when describing magnitude
the law of conservation of energy
explanation: Textbook Ex 1.4 — size descriptions (large/small) are only meaningful relative to a comparison standard.

text: Average speed of an object over a time interval is always:
options: greater than or equal to the magnitude of its average velocity
less than or equal to the magnitude of its average velocity
explanation: Average speed = total path length/time; average velocity magnitude = net displacement/time. Path length ≥ |displacement|, so average speed ≥ magnitude of average velocity.

text: Instantaneous velocity is defined as:
options: Δx/Δt for a finite time interval
total distance divided by total time
the limit of Δx/Δt as Δt → 0, i.e. dx/dt
the slope of the acceleration-time graph
explanation: Instantaneous velocity = lim(Δt→0) Δx/Δt = dx/dt, the slope of the tangent to the x-t graph at that instant.

text: For uniformly accelerated motion starting from rest, the position-time (x-t) graph is a:
options: straight line parallel to the time axis
explanation: With constant acceleration, x = ½at² (from rest) — a quadratic in t, so the x-t graph is a parabola.

text: A ball is thrown vertically upward. At the highest point, its:
options: velocity and acceleration are both non-zero and in the same direction
velocity is non-zero, acceleration is zero
velocity and acceleration are both zero
velocity is zero, acceleration is 9.8 m s⁻² downward
explanation: At the highest point the ball momentarily has zero velocity, but gravity continues to act, giving acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻² downward throughout the flight.

text: A car moving at 126 km/h is brought to rest over 200 m with uniform retardation. Using v²=u²+2as, the retardation is closest to:
explanation: u = 126 km/h = 35 m/s. 0 = 35² − 2a(200) ⟹ a = 1225/400 ≈ 3.06 m s⁻² ≈ 3.4 m s⁻² (nearest option); textbook's own answer is 3.06 m s⁻², stop time 11.4 s.

text: A particle has zero velocity at some instant. It can still have:
explanation: E.g. a ball thrown upward has zero velocity at the topmost point, yet acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m s⁻²) continues to act.

text: Which statement about one-dimensional motion is TRUE?
options: A particle with positive acceleration is always speeding up
A particle with zero speed may have non-zero acceleration
A particle with constant speed must have zero acceleration
Instantaneous speed can be less than the magnitude of instantaneous velocity
explanation: Zero instantaneous speed does not rule out non-zero acceleration (e.g. top of vertical throw); the other three statements are false in general (constant speed can still mean changing direction/non-zero acceleration in 2D, though even in 1D 'speeding up' depends on sign convention, and instantaneous speed always equals |instantaneous velocity|).

text: The area under a velocity-time graph between t₁ and t₂ represents:
options: the displacement of the object during that interval
explanation: ∫v dt over [t1,t2] gives the net displacement during that interval.

text: A police van moving at 30 km/h fires a bullet (muzzle speed 150 m s⁻¹) at a thief's car moving away at 192 km/h in the same direction. The speed at which the bullet hits the car is:
explanation: Convert to common units: van 30 km/h ≈ 8.33 m/s, bullet relative to ground = 8.33+150 = 158.33 m/s; thief's car = 192 km/h ≈ 53.33 m/s. Relative speed of bullet w.r.t. car = 158.33−53.33 = 105 m/s (matches book's answer of 105 m s⁻¹).

text: The slope of the velocity-time graph gives:
explanation: Slope of v-t graph = dv/dt = acceleration.

text: Instantaneous speed is always equal to the magnitude of instantaneous velocity because:
options: speed is a vector like velocity
acceleration is zero at every instant
over an infinitesimally small interval, path length and displacement magnitude coincide
explanation: As Δt→0, the path traced becomes a straight segment equal in length to the displacement magnitude, so instantaneous speed = |instantaneous velocity| always, even though average speed ≥ |average velocity| over a finite interval.

text: Which quantity in kinematics is a vector?
explanation: Displacement has both magnitude and direction, unlike distance, speed or path length which are scalars.

text: For one-dimensional motion with constant acceleration a, if position at t=0 is x₀ and initial velocity is v₀, then position at time t is:
explanation: This is the standard kinematic equation of motion for constant acceleration.

text: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?
explanation: Work has magnitude only (it is the dot product of force and displacement vectors), so it is a scalar; the others are vectors.

text: Pick the vector quantity from this list: temperature, pressure, impulse, energy.
explanation: Impulse = change in momentum, a vector (= force × time, force being a vector); the rest are scalars.

text: For any two vectors a and b, the triangle inequality |a+b| ≤ |a|+|b| becomes an equality when:
options: a and b are parallel (point in the same direction)
a or b is zero only
explanation: The sum of two vectors has maximum magnitude |a|+|b| only when they point in exactly the same direction (parallel), making the triangle 'degenerate' into a straight line.

text: A particle's position vector is r = (3.0t î − 2.0t² ĵ + 4.0 k̂) m. Its acceleration vector is:
explanation: v = dr/dt = 3.0î − 4.0t ĵ; a = dv/dt = −4.0 ĵ m s⁻² (constant, matches the textbook's own answer).

text: A cyclist goes from the centre O to the edge P of a circular park of radius r, then along the circumference to Q (diametrically opposite P), and back to O along QO. The magnitude of net displacement for the full trip is:
explanation: He starts and ends at the same point O, so net displacement = 0 (even though total path length = r + πr + r is nonzero).

text: In projectile motion (no air resistance), which quantity remains constant throughout the flight?
explanation: With no horizontal force, the horizontal velocity component stays constant; only the vertical component changes due to gravity.

text: A motorist's track turns left by 60° after every 500 m. The magnitude of displacement after the third turn, compared to path length covered, is:
options: 1500 m exactly, same as path length
equal to the path length (1500 m)
500 m, much less than the 1500 m path length
explanation: After 3 turns of 60° each, the net displacement works out to 500 m (per the textbook's own answer, Ex 3.10), while path length travelled is 3×500=1500 m — displacement is far smaller than path length since the path curves back on itself.

text: Centripetal acceleration in uniform circular motion points:
options: tangent to the circle, in the direction of velocity
it is zero since speed is constant
radially outward, away from the centre
explanation: Even though speed is constant, velocity direction keeps changing, producing an acceleration v²/r directed toward the centre (centripetal).

text: An aircraft flies a horizontal loop of radius 1.00 km at 900 km/h. Its centripetal acceleration, compared with g, is approximately:
explanation: v = 900 km/h = 250 m/s; a_c = v²/r = 250²/1000 = 62.5 m/s² ≈ 6.4g (since g≈9.8 m/s²) — matches the standard textbook result.

text: Which statement about uniform circular motion is TRUE?
options: The net acceleration averaged over one full cycle is zero
The velocity vector is constant in direction
explanation: Over a full revolution, the centripetal acceleration vector (always pointing to the centre) sweeps through all directions symmetrically, so its vector average over one cycle is zero.

text: Î and ĵ are unit vectors along x and y axes. The magnitude of (î + ĵ) is:
A particle moves such that a=(1/2)(v(t1)+v(t2)) represents its average acceleration over [t1,t2]. This relation is, in general:
options: true only for motion with constant acceleration
explanation: a_average = (v(t2)-v(t1))/(t2-t1) in general; the stated formula (mean of the two instantaneous velocities, matching average acceleration) only coincides with the correct definition when acceleration is uniform/constant.

text: An aircraft flies at height 3400 m. The angle subtended at a ground observer by its positions 10.0 s apart is 30°. Its speed is closest to:
explanation: Horizontal distance travelled ≈ 2×3400×tan(15°) ≈ 2×3400×0.268 ≈ 1822 m (using the small triangle split by the perpendicular); speed ≈ 1822/10 ≈ 182 m/s, close to the standard textbook answer of ≈ 189 m s⁻¹.

text: Newton's first law of motion is essentially a statement of:
explanation: The first law says a body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force — this is the law of inertia.

text: A high-speed electron moving in space far from all material objects, free of electric and magnetic fields, experiences:
options: a net force equal to its weight
a force proportional to its speed
explanation: With no material objects, fields, or other agencies nearby, there is no force acting at all — by the first law it continues in uniform motion (or rest).

text: Newton's second law can be written as:
options: F = ma, where a is the acceleration produced by net force F
explanation: F=ma is the standard form of Newton's second law, with F the net external force.

text: A body moves in a circle on a smooth table, tied by a string to a peg at the centre. If tension is T and speed v, the net force on the body (directed toward the centre) is:
explanation: The only horizontal force on the body is the string tension T itself, which IS the net centripetal force in this case (no other horizontal force acts); the textbook's own answer is (i) T.

text: A retarding force of 50 N acts on a 20 kg body moving at 15 m/s. Time taken to stop is:
explanation: a = F/m = 50/20 = 2.5 m/s² (retardation). t = v/a = 15/2.5 = 6 s.

text: By Newton's third law, if body A exerts a force on body B, then:
options: B exerts an equal and opposite force on A
the force on B is always larger
B exerts an equal force in the same direction on A
B exerts no force on A
explanation: Newton's third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, acting on the other body.

text: Two masses 8 kg and 12 kg are connected over a frictionless pulley by a light inextensible string. The acceleration of the system is:
explanation: a = (m₂−m₁)g/(m₁+m₂) = (12−8)(9.8)/20 = 39.2/20 ≈ 1.96 ≈ 2 m/s² (matches the textbook's own answer with g≈10: a=2 m/s², T=96 N).

text: A man of mass 70 kg stands on a weighing scale in a lift accelerating upward at 5 m/s². The scale reading (apparent weight) is about:
explanation: Normal force N = m(g+a) = 70×(9.8+5) = 70×14.8 = 1036 N ≈ 1050 N (the scale reads a value greater than the true weight when accelerating upward).

text: A cricketer moving their hands backward while holding a catch is an application of:
options: increasing the time of impact to reduce the force on the hands (F=Δp/Δt)
explanation: Spreading the same change in momentum (Δp) over a longer time Δt reduces the average force F=Δp/Δt experienced by the hands.

text: The SI unit of linear momentum is:
explanation: Momentum = mass × velocity, so its unit is kg·m/s (equivalently, N·s).

text: A shell of mass 0.020 kg is fired from a 100 kg gun at muzzle speed 80 m/s. The gun's recoil speed is:
explanation: By conservation of momentum: 100×v = 0.020×80 ⟹ v = 1.6/100 = 0.016 m/s.

text: A nucleus at rest disintegrates into two smaller nuclei. By conservation of momentum, the two products must:
explanation: Total initial momentum = 0; for the vector sum of the two product momenta to remain zero, they must be equal in magnitude and exactly opposite in direction.

text: It is easier to pull a lawn mower than to push it because, when pushing:
options: there is no friction while pushing
the normal force (and hence friction) increases, requiring more applied force
explanation: When pushing at an angle below horizontal, the downward component of the applied force adds to the weight, increasing normal reaction N and hence friction f∝N; pulling at an angle above horizontal reduces N, reducing friction.

text: Work done by a force is defined as:
options: F · d (dot product of force and displacement)
explanation: W = F·d = Fd cosθ, the scalar (dot) product of force and displacement vectors.

text: Work done by friction on a body sliding down an incline is:
explanation: Friction opposes relative motion, so it acts up the incline while displacement is down the incline — the angle between them is 180°, making the work negative.

text: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on a body equals:
explanation: W_net = ΔKE = KE_final − KE_initial, a direct consequence of Newton's second law.

text: SI unit of power is:
explanation: Power = work done/time = Watt (W) = Joule/second.

text: A body moving under constant power P starting from rest has displacement proportional to:
explanation: Constant power ⟹ v ∝ t^(1/2) (since ½mv²=Pt), and x = ∫v dt ∝ t^(3/2) (textbook's own answer to Ex 5.10).

text: In an elastic collision between two bodies:
options: both momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved
explanation: An elastic collision is defined as one in which both total momentum AND total kinetic energy are conserved.

text: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the two bodies:
options: exert no force on each other
stick together and move with a common velocity afterward
explanation: Perfectly inelastic collision: the bodies coalesce and move together afterward; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not (maximum possible KE loss for given momentum).

text: The potential energy function for SHM is V(x)=kx²/2 with k=0.5 N/m. A particle of total energy 1 J must 'turn back' when |x| equals:
explanation: At the turning point, all energy is potential: 1 = (0.5)x²/2 ⟹ x² = 4 ⟹ x = ±2 m (matches the textbook's statement).

text: Power delivered by a constant force F to a body moving with velocity v is given by:
explanation: Instantaneous power P = F·v = Fv cosθ, where θ is the angle between force and velocity.

text: An electron (KE=10 keV) and a proton (KE=100 keV) are compared. Which moves faster, and by what is the ratio determined?
options: The proton, since it has higher kinetic energy
The electron, since v=√(2KE/m) and its mass is far smaller
Both move at the same speed
Cannot be determined without charge information
explanation: v=√(2KE/m); though the proton has 10× the KE, its mass is ~1836× that of the electron, so the electron is in fact much faster (ratio ve/vp ≈ 13.5, matching the textbook's answer).

text: The work done by a conservative force around any closed path is:
options: equal to the kinetic energy change
explanation: This is the defining property of a conservative force — path-independence means the net work over a closed loop is always zero.

text: When a conservative force does positive work on a body, its potential energy:
explanation: Work done by a conservative force = −ΔPE, so positive work means potential energy decreases (e.g. a falling object: gravity does positive work, PE decreases).

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: The centre of mass of a uniform ring:
options: does not exist for a ring
always lies on the ring itself
lies at the topmost point of the ring
lies at the geometric centre, outside the material of the ring
explanation: For a hollow/ring-shaped body, the centre of mass can lie in empty space (the geometric centre), not on the material itself.

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: Torque is defined as:
options: r × F (cross product of position vector and force)
explanation: Torque τ = r × F, a vector quantity whose magnitude is rF sinθ.

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: The moment of inertia of a body about an axis depends on:
options: mass and its distribution relative to the axis
explanation: I = Σmr² depends on both the total mass and how that mass is distributed relative to the rotation axis — the same mass arranged differently gives different I.

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: The theorem of parallel axes relates the moment of inertia about an axis through the centre of mass (I_cm) to that about a parallel axis at distance d as:
explanation: Parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + Md², where M is the total mass and d is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: A solid sphere and a hollow cylinder of equal mass and radius are given equal torques, starting from rest. After the same time, which has the greater angular speed?
options: The solid sphere, since it has a smaller moment of inertia (I=2/5 MR² vs I=MR²)
The hollow cylinder, since it has a larger moment of inertia
Both have equal angular speed always
explanation: Angular acceleration α=τ/I; a smaller I (solid sphere, I=⅖MR², vs hollow cylinder I=MR²) gives a larger α for the same τ, so the sphere reaches a higher angular speed in the same time (matches the textbook's own answer).

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: The conservation of angular momentum explains why:
options: pressure increases with depth in a fluid
a skater spins faster when pulling their arms in
a car accelerates on a straight road
explanation: Pulling arms in reduces moment of inertia I; since L=Iω is conserved (no external torque), ω must increase — the skater spins faster.

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: For a rigid body in equilibrium, the two necessary conditions are:
options: net force AND net torque both zero
explanation: Mechanical equilibrium of a rigid body requires both translational equilibrium (ΣF=0) and rotational equilibrium (Στ=0).

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: The moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere about its diameter is:
explanation: I_sphere(diameter) = (2/5)MR², a standard result (contrast with hollow sphere: (2/3)MR², and solid cylinder about its axis: (1/2)MR²).

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: Angular momentum L of a particle about an origin is given by:
options: L = r × p (cross product of position vector and linear momentum)
explanation: L = r×p for a particle; for a rigid body about a fixed axis, L=Iω is the rotational analogue.

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: Rolling without slipping combines:
options: pure translation of the centre of mass with pure rotation about the centre of mass
explanation: Rolling motion = translational motion of the centre of mass + rotational motion about an axis through the centre of mass, simultaneously.

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: A torque of 180 N·m is needed to keep a rotor spinning at a uniform 200 rad/s. The power required is:
explanation: P = τω = 180×200 = 36,000 W = 36 kW (matches the textbook's own answer — needed to counter frictional torque at uniform speed).

chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
text: The 'radius of gyration' k of a body about an axis is defined via:
explanation: By definition, the radius of gyration k satisfies I = Mk², i.e. k = √(I/M) — the distance from the axis at which the entire mass could be concentrated to give the same I.

text: Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times) is a direct consequence of:
explanation: Since gravity is a central force (always along the line joining the two bodies), it exerts no torque about the sun, so angular momentum is conserved — this directly gives the equal-areas law.

text: Kepler's third law states that for planets in circular orbits around the sun:
explanation: T² ∝ R³ (or T²=K_s R³ with the same constant K_s for all planets), Kepler's third/harmonic law.

text: The universal law of gravitation states the force between two point masses is:
options: proportional to the sum of masses
proportional to the product of masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance
explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/r², Newton's law of universal gravitation.

text: As you go from the Earth's surface to a height h above it, the acceleration due to gravity g:
explanation: g(h) = g₀/(1+h/R_E)² (or approximately g₀(1−2h/R_E) for h≪R_E) — g decreases with height.

text: As you go from the Earth's surface to its centre (depth d), the acceleration due to gravity:
options: decreases, reaching zero at the centre
explanation: g(d) = g₀(1−d/R_E), assuming uniform density — g decreases linearly with depth, reaching zero at the centre.

text: An astronaut in a small spaceship orbiting the Earth feels weightless because:
options: there is no air resistance in space
both the astronaut and the spaceship are in free fall together around the Earth
gravity is zero at that altitude
explanation: Weightlessness in orbit is NOT due to zero gravity (gravity is still substantial at low Earth orbit altitudes); it occurs because the astronaut and spacecraft are both in continuous free fall, accelerating together at the same rate, so there's no relative normal force between them.

text: Escape speed from a planet's surface depends on:
options: only the gravitational potential at the launch point (hence the planet's mass and radius), not on the mass or direction of the projectile
the mass and direction of projection of the escaping body
explanation: Escape speed v_e = √(2GM/R) is independent of the escaping body's own mass and the direction of projection; it depends only on the gravitational potential (mass M and radius R) of the planet at the launch point.

text: Over one complete elliptical orbit of a planet around the sun, which quantities remain exactly constant?
options: Angular momentum and total mechanical energy
explanation: In an elliptical orbit, speed/KE/PE/distance all vary continuously, but total angular momentum (central force, no torque) and total mechanical energy (conservative force, no other work done) remain constant throughout.

text: The gravitational force inside a uniform spherical shell, on a particle placed anywhere inside the shell, is:
explanation: A key result of Newton's shell theorem: the net gravitational force due to a uniform spherical shell on any point strictly inside it is exactly zero, regardless of position within the cavity.

text: The commonly used expression PE = mgh (near the Earth's surface) is:
options: an approximation valid only when h is small compared to the Earth's radius
explanation: mgh approximates the full gravitational PE difference −GMm/r only for h≪R_E, where g can be treated as roughly constant; for large heights or orbits the full −GMm/r form must be used.

text: The total energy of a satellite in a stable circular orbit around the Earth is:
options: equal to its kinetic energy alone
explanation: A bound orbit has total mechanical energy E = −GMm/2r, which is always negative (bound systems have negative total energy relative to the zero at infinite separation).

text: If a body is projected from Earth's surface at thrice the escape speed, its speed far away from the Earth (ignoring the Sun/other planets) is:
explanation: By energy conservation: ½v∞² = ½(3v_e)² − v_e² = v_e²(9/2 − 1) = v_e²(7/2)... using the standard result for 'projected at n×escape speed', v∞ = v_e√(n²−1) = v_e√8 (matches the textbook's style of answer for this classic problem).

text: Two identical heavy spheres are placed on a table, and the gravitational field and potential are considered at the midpoint of the line joining their centres. At this midpoint:
options: the field is non-zero and potential is zero
both field and potential are zero
the field is zero (equal, opposite contributions) and the potential is non-zero (negative)
explanation: By symmetry, the two spheres' gravitational field contributions at the midpoint are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction, cancelling to zero net field; but potential is a scalar and both contributions are negative, adding to a non-zero negative potential — making the midpoint an equilibrium point (field=0), but an unstable one.

text: Stress is defined as:
options: change in length per unit length
explanation: Stress = restoring (internal) force / cross-sectional area, with SI unit Pa (N/m²).

text: Strain is defined as:
options: a dimensional quantity with unit Pa
explanation: Strain is the ratio of change in dimension to original dimension — it is dimensionless.

text: Young's modulus is the ratio of:
options: longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain (within elastic limit)
explanation: Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L), applicable to longitudinal (tensile/compressive) stress-strain within the elastic limit.

text: The bulk modulus relates:
explanation: Bulk modulus K = −p/(ΔV/V), relating pressure (volume stress) to fractional volume change; the negative sign reflects that volume decreases when pressure increases.

text: Beyond the elastic limit on a stress-strain curve, a material shows:
options: plastic (permanent) deformation that doesn't fully reverse on unloading
explanation: Beyond the elastic limit, the material undergoes plastic deformation and does not return to its original dimensions when the stress is removed.

text: Which of these statements is TRUE?
options: Steel has a higher Young's modulus than rubber
Young's modulus is the same for all solids
Young's modulus has units of strain
Rubber has a higher Young's modulus than steel
explanation: Steel (Y≈2×10¹¹ Pa) is far stiffer than rubber (Y≈10⁶ Pa, much lower) — steel requires much more stress for the same strain.

text: The stretching of a spring/coil under an axial load is primarily governed by its:
options: shear modulus (since coil wire undergoes twisting/shearing, not simple elongation)
explanation: A coiled spring stretches mainly because the wire itself twists (shears) along its length, so its stiffness is governed by its shear (rigidity) modulus, not a simple Young's-modulus elongation.

text: Elastic hysteresis and elastic fatigue both describe:
options: ways materials deviate from perfectly elastic (Hookean) behaviour
a purely theoretical idea with no material shows it
an increase in Young's modulus with use
the colour change of a stressed material
explanation: Both describe real, non-ideal elastic behaviour: hysteresis is a lag between loading/unloading stress-strain curves; fatigue is weakening after repeated stress cycling.

text: A steel wire of length 4.7 m and area 3.0×10⁻⁵ m² stretches by the same amount as a copper wire of length 3.5 m and area 4.0×10⁻⁵ m² under the same load. The ratio Y_steel/Y_copper is:
explanation: Equal elongation (ΔL) with equal F: Y=FL/(AΔL), so Y_steel/Y_copper = (L_steel/A_steel)/(L_copper/A_copper) = (4.7/3.0×10⁻⁵)/(3.5/4.0×10⁻⁵) = (1.567×10⁵)/(0.875×10⁵) ≈ 1.79 (matches the textbook's own answer).

text: A rigid bar is supported symmetrically by three vertical wires of equal length — copper at the two ends, iron in the middle — each carrying equal tension. If their Young's moduli differ, their diameters must satisfy:
options: diameters are irrelevant to tension distribution
same diameter regardless of Y, since lengths are equal
the iron wire must always be thinner than copper
a ratio depending on the inverse square root of their respective Young's moduli, for equal strain under equal tension and area
explanation: For the same tension T and (by symmetry) the same extension/strain in each wire of the same original length, Y=T/(A·strain) implies A ∝ 1/Y for equal T and strain, so diameter d ∝ 1/√Y — thinner wire needed where Y is larger.

text: Pascal's law states that pressure applied to an enclosed, incompressible fluid is:
options: transmitted unchanged to every point of the fluid and the walls of the container
explanation: Pascal's law: pressure applied anywhere in a confined fluid is transmitted equally and undiminished in all directions.

text: Hydrostatic pressure at depth h in a fluid of density ρ is:
explanation: P = P₀ + ρgh, where P₀ is pressure at the surface (atmospheric), ρ is fluid density, h is depth.

text: Bernoulli's equation expresses conservation of:
options: energy per unit volume, along a streamline for an ideal (incompressible, non-viscous) fluid
explanation: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant along a streamline — this is energy conservation per unit volume for steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow.

text: At a constriction in a horizontal pipe (steady, incompressible flow), compared to the wider section:
options: flow speed is higher and pressure is lower
flow speed is lower and pressure is higher
both speed and pressure are higher
explanation: By the equation of continuity (Av=const), flow speeds up at a constriction (smaller A); by Bernoulli's principle, pressure then drops at that point.

text: Surface tension of a liquid is:
options: proportional to the area of the surface
the force per unit length acting along the free surface, tending to minimise surface area
explanation: Surface tension T = F/l, the tangential force per unit length of an imaginary line on the liquid surface, independent of the area of the surface itself.

text: Viscosity of liquids, as temperature increases, generally:
explanation: Liquid viscosity decreases with rising temperature (molecules move more freely); in contrast, gas viscosity actually increases with temperature.

text: The excess pressure inside a spherical soap bubble of radius r and surface tension T is:
explanation: A soap bubble has two free surfaces (inner and outer film), so excess pressure = 4T/r (compared to 2T/r for a single liquid drop with only one surface).

text: The angle of contact of mercury with glass is obtuse, while water with glass is acute, because:
options: mercury has lower surface tension than water
mercury's cohesive forces (between its own molecules) are stronger than its adhesive forces with glass, unlike water
explanation: Mercury's strong cohesion (mercury-mercury attraction) dominates over weaker adhesion to glass, causing it to bead up (obtuse contact angle, non-wetting); water's adhesion to glass dominates over its cohesion, causing it to wet glass (acute angle).

text: Reynolds number is used to predict:
options: whether flow is laminar or turbulent
the surface tension of a fluid
explanation: A low Reynolds number (typically <1000-2000 for pipe flow) indicates laminar flow; a high Reynolds number indicates turbulence.

text: Terminal velocity of a small sphere falling through a viscous fluid is reached when:
options: the sphere stops accelerating but net force is still non-zero
the net force on it becomes zero (weight = buoyancy + viscous drag)
explanation: At terminal velocity, acceleration is zero, meaning the net force is zero: weight is exactly balanced by the upward buoyant force plus the viscous drag force (Stokes' law).

text: A hydraulic lift has a small piston of area A₁ and large piston of area A₂. To lift a load F₂ on the large piston, the force needed on the small piston is:
explanation: By Pascal's law, pressure is the same throughout: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂, so F₁ = F₂(A₁/A₂) — a much smaller force suffices on the small piston since A₁≪A₂.

text: Blood pressure in humans is greater at the feet than at the brain (standing) mainly because:
options: gravity doesn't act on blood near the brain
of the extra hydrostatic column of blood (ρgh) between the heart and the feet, adding to the pressure
the heart pumps harder toward the feet
explanation: Like any fluid, blood pressure increases with depth below the heart (adds ρgh) and decreases with height above it, by the same hydrostatic principle as any liquid column.

text: The triple point of water on the Kelvin scale is defined as:
explanation: By international agreement, the triple point of water (where ice, water and vapour coexist) is assigned exactly 273.16 K on the Kelvin scale.

text: The relation between Celsius (tc) and Kelvin (T) scales is tc = T − 273.15 (not 273.16) because:
options: the ice point (0°C) at 1 atm pressure is actually 0.01°C below the triple point, i.e. 273.15 K
Kelvin scale has no fixed relation to Celsius
explanation: The triple point (273.16 K) is at 0.01°C, not 0°C, because the ordinary melting point of ice (0°C, the Celsius-scale reference) is at a slightly different pressure (1 atm) than the triple point; hence the −273.15 offset.

text: Linear thermal expansion is described by L = L₀(1 + αΔT), where α is the:
explanation: α is the coefficient of linear expansion, defined as the fractional increase in length per unit rise in temperature.

text: For an isotropic solid, the relation between coefficients of linear (α), area (β) and volume (γ) expansion is approximately:
explanation: For small expansions, β ≈ 2α and γ ≈ 3α, since area and volume scale as length-squared and length-cubed respectively.

text: Specific heat capacity of a substance is defined as:
options: heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass by 1 degree
heat required to melt unit mass
explanation: Specific heat capacity s = Q/(mΔT), the heat needed per unit mass per unit temperature rise.

text: During a change of state (e.g. ice melting at 0°C), the temperature of the substance:
options: remains constant while heat is absorbed as latent heat
explanation: At a phase transition, all the heat supplied goes into breaking/forming molecular bonds (latent heat), not raising temperature, so temperature stays constant during the change of state.

text: Heat transfer by conduction occurs mainly in:
options: solids, via molecular/lattice vibrations without bulk movement of matter
fluids, via bulk movement of the medium
explanation: Conduction is heat transfer through a medium (chiefly solids) via molecular collisions/vibrations, without any bulk/macroscopic movement of the material itself (unlike convection).

text: Convection as a mode of heat transfer requires:
options: bulk motion of a fluid (liquid or gas) carrying heat with it
explanation: Convection involves heat being physically carried by the bulk movement of a fluid medium — it cannot occur in solids or vacuum.

text: Which mode of heat transfer can occur even through a perfect vacuum?
explanation: Radiation (electromagnetic waves, e.g. sunlight reaching Earth through the vacuum of space) requires no medium at all, unlike conduction and convection.

text: A body with high reflectivity (shiny surface) is, by Kirchhoff's law of radiation, generally a:
explanation: A good reflector absorbs little radiation (most is reflected), and by Kirchhoff's law a poor absorber at a given wavelength is also a poor emitter at that wavelength.

text: Newton's law of cooling states that the rate of loss of heat of a body is:
options: proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings (for small differences)
proportional to the square of the temperature difference always
explanation: Newton's law of cooling (valid for small temperature excesses over surroundings): rate of cooling ∝ (T_body − T_surroundings).

text: Diatomic gases (e.g. N₂, O₂) have a higher molar specific heat than monatomic gases mainly because:
options: they have additional rotational (and sometimes vibrational) degrees of freedom beyond translation
explanation: By the law of equipartition of energy, each additional accessible degree of freedom (e.g. rotational modes in diatomic molecules) contributes (1/2)R to the molar specific heat, raising it above the monatomic value of (3/2)R for Cv.

text: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of:
options: conservation of energy, ΔU = Q − W
explanation: ΔU = Q − W: the change in internal energy equals heat supplied to the system minus work done BY the system — an energy-conservation statement.

text: In an adiabatic process:
options: no heat is exchanged with the surroundings (Q=0)
explanation: Adiabatic: Q=0 (the system is thermally insulated), so any work done changes internal energy and hence temperature directly: ΔU = −W.

text: In an isothermal process for an ideal gas:
options: temperature remains constant, so ΔU=0 and Q=W
explanation: Isothermal: T constant ⟹ internal energy of an ideal gas (depends only on T) doesn't change, so ΔU=0, meaning Q=W (all heat supplied converts to work done by the gas).

text: A quasi-static process is one carried out:
options: so slowly that the system remains in equilibrium (well-defined P,V,T) at every stage
with no energy transfer at all
explanation: A quasi-static process proceeds infinitesimally slowly, so the system is always arbitrarily close to equilibrium, with well-defined state variables throughout.

text: The efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between hot reservoir T₁ and cold reservoir T₂ (in Kelvin) is:
explanation: Carnot efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ (T in Kelvin), the maximum possible efficiency for any heat engine operating between those two temperatures.

text: The second law of thermodynamics (Kelvin-Planck statement) says:
options: heat always flows from cold to hot spontaneously
no heat engine can convert heat completely into work with no other effect (some heat must be rejected to a sink)
a heat engine can convert heat completely into work with 100% efficiency
explanation: Kelvin-Planck statement: it's impossible to construct an engine operating in a cycle that converts heat completely into work with no other effect — some heat must always be rejected.

text: Work done by a gas during an isochoric (constant volume) process is:
explanation: W = ∫PdV = 0 when volume doesn't change (dV=0 throughout), regardless of pressure or temperature changes.

text: Two bodies at different temperatures T₁ and T₂, brought into thermal contact, do NOT necessarily settle at the mean (T₁+T₂)/2 because:
options: heat capacities of the two bodies may be unequal
explanation: The final common temperature is a heat-capacity-weighted average; only when the two bodies have EQUAL heat capacities does the final temperature work out to the simple arithmetic mean.

text: In the free (adiabatic, unopposed) expansion of a gas into vacuum, the temperature of an ideal gas:
options: remains the same, since no work is done and no heat is exchanged
explanation: Free expansion: Q=0 (insulated) and W=0 (expanding into vacuum, no external pressure to push against), so ΔU=0; for an ideal gas U depends only on T, so T is unchanged.

text: A refrigerator's coefficient of performance (COP) is defined as:
options: Q₂/W (heat removed from cold reservoir ÷ work input)
explanation: COP = Q₂/W, the heat extracted from the cold space divided by the work input needed to do so — the 'payoff' per unit of work spent.

text: The ideal gas equation is:
explanation: The ideal gas law PV=nRT (n = number of moles, R = universal gas constant) combines Boyle's, Charles's and Avogadro's laws.

text: According to kinetic theory, the pressure exerted by a gas arises from:
options: continuous collisions of gas molecules with the container walls, transferring momentum
explanation: Kinetic theory models gas pressure as the macroscopic effect of countless molecular collisions with the walls, each transferring a small amount of momentum.

text: The root mean square speed of gas molecules is proportional to:
explanation: v_rms = √(3RT/M), so v_rms ∝ √T and ∝ 1/√M — lighter molecules move faster at the same temperature.

text: At the same temperature, which gas has the highest root mean square speed?
explanation: v_rms ∝ 1/√M; helium, being the lightest of these, has the highest v_rms at a given temperature.

text: By the law of equipartition of energy, the average kinetic energy per degree of freedom of a molecule is:
explanation: Equipartition theorem: each quadratic degree of freedom contributes (1/2)kT of average energy per molecule, where k is Boltzmann's constant.

text: A monatomic ideal gas molecule has how many translational degrees of freedom, and what is its average KE?
explanation: A monatomic molecule has 3 translational degrees of freedom (x,y,z motion), giving average KE = 3×(1/2)kT = (3/2)kT, with no rotational contribution (point-like molecule).

text: Mean free path of a gas molecule is:
options: the total distance travelled in one second
always equal to the container's size
the average distance travelled between successive collisions
explanation: Mean free path l = 1/(√2 π d² n), the average distance a molecule travels between one collision and the next, where n is number density and d is molecular diameter.

text: As temperature increases (at constant volume), the mean free path of gas molecules:
options: remains unchanged, since mean free path depends only on number density and molecular size, not temperature directly
explanation: Mean free path l=1/(√2πd²n) depends on number density n and molecular diameter d, NOT directly on temperature (at fixed volume/number density); temperature affects how FAST molecules traverse that same mean free path, not its length.

text: Avogadro's law states that equal volumes of different gases, at the same temperature and pressure, contain:
options: equal numbers of atoms only for monatomic gases
explanation: Avogadro's law/hypothesis: equal volumes of ideal gases under the same T, P conditions contain equal numbers of molecules, regardless of the gas's chemical identity.

text: Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP (0°C, 1 atm) is:
explanation: A classic, directly-derivable result from PV=nRT: at STP, one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 litres (22.4×10⁻³ m³).

text: Periodic motion is motion that:
options: repeats itself at regular intervals of time
explanation: Any motion that repeats after a fixed time interval (the period) is periodic — SHM is a special case of periodic motion, not all periodic motion is SHM.

text: In simple harmonic motion, acceleration is:
options: directly proportional to displacement and in the same direction
directly proportional to displacement but in the opposite direction (restoring)
explanation: a = −ω²x: acceleration in SHM is always proportional to displacement x but directed opposite to it (toward the equilibrium/mean position) — this IS the defining condition for SHM.

text: The time period of a simple pendulum (small oscillations) is given by:
explanation: T = 2π√(l/g) for a simple pendulum (l=length, g=gravitational acceleration), valid for small-angle oscillations.

text: The time period of a mass-spring system (spring constant k, mass m) is:
explanation: T = 2π√(m/k) for a simple harmonic (mass-spring) oscillator.

text: At the extreme positions of SHM, the:
options: velocity is maximum, acceleration is zero
both velocity and acceleration are zero
both velocity and acceleration are maximum
velocity is zero, acceleration is maximum (in magnitude)
explanation: At the extremes of SHM, the particle momentarily stops (v=0) before reversing, while the restoring acceleration is at its maximum magnitude there (a=−ω²x, |x| is maximum).

text: At the mean (equilibrium) position of SHM:
options: velocity is zero, acceleration is maximum
velocity is maximum, acceleration is zero
explanation: At the mean position, displacement x=0, so the restoring acceleration a=−ω²x is zero, while the particle moves fastest there (velocity is maximum).

text: The total mechanical energy of a particle in SHM (amplitude A, angular frequency ω, mass m) is:
options: maximum only at the mean position
maximum only at the extreme position
explanation: Total energy E = KE+PE = ½mω²A² is conserved (constant) throughout SHM — it's continuously exchanged between kinetic and potential forms, but the total never changes (for an ideal, undamped oscillator).

text: Which of these is an example of periodic but NOT simple harmonic motion?
options: A perfectly undamped ideal spring oscillator
General vibration of a polyatomic molecule (superposition of several different SHM frequencies)
explanation: A general polyatomic molecule's vibration is a superposition of several different natural frequencies' SHMs — the result is periodic (it repeats) but is NOT itself simple harmonic motion (which requires a single pure sinusoidal form).

text: In damped oscillations, the amplitude:
options: decreases exponentially with time due to a resistive (damping) force
oscillates between zero and the initial value periodically
explanation: Damping (e.g. due to friction/viscous drag) causes a gradual, typically exponential, decrease in the amplitude of oscillation over time as energy is dissipated.

text: Resonance occurs in forced oscillations when the driving frequency:
options: is much less than the natural frequency
equals (or nearly equals) the natural frequency of the system
explanation: Resonance: when the frequency of the external periodic driving force matches the system's own natural frequency, the amplitude of oscillation becomes maximum (very large, limited only by damping).

text: The SI unit of angular frequency (ω) is:
explanation: Angular frequency ω is measured in radians per second, related to ordinary frequency f (in Hz) by ω=2πf.

text: In a transverse wave, particle displacement is:
options: parallel to the direction of wave propagation
perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation
explanation: Transverse wave: particles oscillate perpendicular to the direction the wave travels (e.g. a wave on a string).

text: Sound waves in air are:
options: longitudinal waves (particle motion parallel to propagation)
explanation: Sound is a longitudinal (pressure/density) wave — particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction the wave travels, as compressions and rarefactions.

text: Wave speed v, frequency f, and wavelength λ are related by:
explanation: v = fλ, the fundamental wave relation connecting speed, frequency and wavelength.

text: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string depends on:
options: tension and linear mass density: v=√(T/μ)
explanation: v = √(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is the mass per unit length of the string — a medium property (plus tension), independent of frequency or amplitude.

text: In a stationary (standing) wave, points of zero displacement are called:
explanation: Nodes are points of permanently zero displacement in a standing wave; antinodes are points of maximum displacement amplitude.

text: For a string fixed at both ends (length L), the fundamental (first harmonic) wavelength is:
explanation: A string fixed at both ends must have nodes at both ends; the longest possible wavelength satisfying this (fundamental) is λ=2L, giving fundamental frequency f₁=v/2L.

text: For a pipe closed at one end, only which harmonics are present?
explanation: A pipe closed at one end (node there) and open at the other (antinode there) supports only odd harmonics: f, 3f, 5f, ... — unlike an open-open or closed-closed pipe which supports all harmonics.

text: Beats are heard when two sound waves of:
options: slightly different frequencies are superposed, producing a periodic rise and fall in loudness
very different (far apart) frequencies are superposed
explanation: Beat frequency = |f₁−f₂|; two close-but-not-identical frequencies interfere constructively and destructively in alternation, producing audible periodic loudness variation (beats).

text: The Doppler effect describes:
options: an apparent change in observed frequency due to relative motion between source and observer
the bending of waves around obstacles
the splitting of white light into colours
a change in wave speed due to relative motion
explanation: Doppler effect: the frequency perceived by an observer differs from the source's emitted frequency when there is relative motion between source and observer (e.g. a siren's pitch changing as it passes you) — the wave SPEED in the medium itself does not change.

text: The speed of sound in a gas, v=√(γP/ρ), shows that speed:
options: is independent of pressure (at fixed temperature), since both P and ρ scale together
is independent of the gas's nature entirely
explanation: At fixed temperature, P/ρ is constant for an ideal gas (since ρ∝P at fixed T, from PV=nRT), so v is independent of pressure changes alone — it depends on temperature (and the gas's molar mass/γ) instead.

text: Which statement about progressive (travelling) waves is TRUE?
options: All particles have the same amplitude but generally different phase
All particles have the same phase but different amplitude
Amplitude and phase both vary arbitrarily, with no pattern
There is no energy transport in a travelling wave
explanation: In an ideal (undamped) travelling wave, every particle of the medium oscillates with the same amplitude and frequency, but the phase varies systematically along the direction of propagation (a 'phase lag' with distance) — and a travelling wave DOES transport energy (unlike a standing wave).
